summary: bend angle (θ) is what the Bend allowance calculator works out, and it gets there from the inside radius, the material thickness and the bend allowance. That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Bend allowance calculator work?
sections.html:
The Bend allowance calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports bend angle (θ) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the inside radius (r), the material thickness (T) and the bend allowance (BA).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Bend allowance calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Bend angle (θ)=180 × bend allowance (BA) ÷ (PI × (inside radius (r) + k-factor × material thickness (T)))
Bend deduction (BD)=-bend allowance (BA) + 2 × inside radius (r) × the tangent of ((1 ÷ 360) × PI × bend angle (θ)) + 2 × material thickness (T) × the tangent of ((1 ÷ 360) × PI × bend angle (θ))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Inside radius (r) = 30 mm, Material thickness (T) = 30 mm and K-factor = 10. The calculator returns Bend angle (θ) = 298.4369 deg, Bend allowance (BA) = 30 mm and Bend deduction (BD) = -24.5417 mm.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Bend angle (θ) = 298.4369 deg, Bend allowance (BA) = 30 mm and Bend deduction (BD) = -24.5417 mm should be roughly the size you expected from Inside radius (r) = 30 mm and Material thickness (T) = 30 mm.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Length, opening in millimeters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Bend allowance calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the inside radius, the material thickness and the bend allowance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Bend allowance calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns bend angle (θ), derived from the inside radius, the material thickness and the bend allowance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Bend allowance calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the inside radius, the material thickness and the bend allowance, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter bend angle (θ) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Bend angle (θ) opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Bend angle (θ) = 298.4369 deg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Bend allowance calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
